chapters.title: Chapter 1: What Commodities Are and Why They Trade

lessons.title: Hedgers, Speculators and Arbitrageurs: Who Is on the Other Side of Your Trade

children.text: Every time you buy a commodity futures contract, someone sells it to you. On MCX, that someone might be a Rajkot jeweller locking in the cost of gold for wedding season orders, a professional trader betting the other way, or a bullion dealer quietly pocketing a price gap between two markets. Knowing who is on the other side of your trade, and why they are there, is one of the most useful things a new commodity trader can learn. By the end of this lesson you will know the three kinds of market participants, how each one uses futures, and why this mix is what keeps commodity markets working.

body.text: Hedgers come to the market to get rid of price risk. Speculators come to take that risk on in exchange for potential profit. Arbitrageurs keep prices honest by exploiting small gaps between markets. Every liquid commodity market needs all three.

markDefs.definition: An exchange-traded agreement to buy or sell a standard quantity of a commodity at a price fixed today, for settlement on a future date.

children.text: You will study futures mechanics properly in Chapter 2. For this lesson, you only need one idea: a
futures contract
lets you fix a price today for a trade that settles on a later date. If the price rises, the buyer of the futures gains and the seller loses. If it falls, the reverse happens.
Hedgers: Businesses Shedding Price Risk

markDefs.definition: A market participant who takes a futures position to offset the price risk of a physical business exposure they already have or will have.

children.text: A
hedger
already has exposure to a commodity through their business, and uses futures to neutralise it. There are two kinds.
The Long Hedge: A Jeweller Who Must Buy Later

Suresh runs a jewellery manufacturing unit in Rajkot. In September, he accepts wedding season orders at fixed prices, and he will need to buy 1 kg of gold in November to make them. Gold is at ₹1,00,000 per 10 grams today (an illustrative price). If gold rises by November, his profit margin disappears.

markDefs.definition: Buying futures to protect against a rise in the price of a commodity you will need to buy in the future.

children.text: So he buys gold futures covering 1 kg at ₹1,00,000 per 10 grams. This is a
long hedge

body.caption: Suresh's long gold futures at ₹1,00,000 per 10 grams. The futures gain as gold rises, exactly offsetting the higher cost of the physical gold he must buy.

body.title: Suresh's cost of 1 kg gold in November (₹ lakh)
body.xAxisLabel: Gold price in November (₹ per 10 grams)

children.text: If gold rises to ₹1,05,000, his physical gold costs ₹5,000 more per 10 grams, which is ₹5,00,000 more for 1 kg. His futures gain ₹5,000 per 10 grams, also ₹5,00,000. The two cancel out, and his net cost stays at ₹1 crore. If gold falls, he pays less for physical gold but loses on futures. Either way, his cost is locked.
The Short Hedge: A Stockist Who Must Sell Later

markDefs.definition: Selling futures to protect against a fall in the price of a commodity you own or will produce.

children.text: Kantibhai, a jeera stockist in Unjha, holds 10 tonnes (100 quintals) of jeera he plans to sell over the next two months. Jeera is at ₹24,000 per quintal (illustrative). A good crop elsewhere could push prices down before he sells. So he sells NCDEX jeera futures covering 100 quintals at ₹24,000. This is a
short hedge

body.caption: Kantibhai's short jeera futures at ₹24,000 per quintal. The futures gain as jeera falls, offsetting the lower value of his physical stock.
Kantibhai's outcome on 100 quintals if jeera falls to ₹21,000

body.text: A hedge is not meant to make money. Its job is to make the outcome predictable. A hedger who loses on futures because prices moved in their favour physically has not made a mistake. They paid for certainty, exactly as you pay for insurance and are glad your house did not burn down.

body.title: Why real hedges are never perfect: basis risk

markDefs.definition: The difference between the local spot price of a commodity and the price of the related futures contract.

children.text: The examples above assume the physical price and the futures price move exactly together. In real life they do not, and the gap between them is called
basis
Suresh makes 22 karat jewellery, but MCX gold is 995 purity. The two prices track closely, not perfectly.
Kantibhai's jeera may be a different grade from the contract specification, and local mandi prices can diverge from NCDEX.
Hedge timing rarely matches expiry dates exactly, so hedgers often close or roll positions early.
A hedge removes most of the price risk, but the leftover basis risk means the final result can be somewhat better or worse than the locked-in price. You will learn how basis behaves in Chapter 2.
Speculators: Taking Risk for Profit

markDefs.definition: A market participant with no physical exposure who takes futures positions purely to profit from expected price movements.

children.text: A
speculator
has no physical gold, jeera or crude to protect. They trade purely on a view of where prices are going. Most retail commodity traders are speculators.
Rohit, a 31-year-old analyst in Indore, expects OPEC+ to announce production cuts. He buys one lot of MCX Crude Oil Mini, which covers 10 barrels, at ₹6,500 per barrel (illustrative).
If crude rises to ₹6,800: gain of ₹300 × 10 barrels = ₹3,000
If crude falls to ₹6,150: loss of ₹350 × 10 barrels = ₹3,500

markDefs.definition: How easily you can buy or sell without moving the price much. Liquid markets have many active buyers and sellers and narrow bid-ask spreads.

children.text: Speculators are often blamed for price spikes, but markets cannot function without them. When Kantibhai wants to sell jeera futures, someone must buy. Another hedger who needs jeera may not show up that day. A speculator willing to take the other side supplies the
liquidity
that lets hedgers get in and out at fair prices.

columns.label: Hedger
points: Has a physical exposure through their business
Measures success by predictability of cost or revenue
Accepts futures losses when the physical side gains
Examples: jewellers, stockists, processors, farmer producer organisations

columns.label: Speculator
points: Uses futures to take on risk
Measures success purely by trading profit
A losing position is a real loss, with nothing to offset it
Examples: retail traders, proprietary trading desks

body.title: Rohit's crude trade
body.prompt: Rohit buys 2 lots of MCX Crude Oil Mini (10 barrels each) at ₹6,420 per barrel. He exits when crude reaches ₹6,275. Ignoring costs, what is his profit or loss in rupees? Enter a loss as a negative number.
body.explanation: Price change = ₹6,275 minus ₹6,420 = minus ₹145 per barrel. Quantity = 2 lots × 10 barrels = 20 barrels. Loss = minus ₹145 × 20 = minus ₹2,900. With no physical crude to offset it, the full ₹2,900 is a real loss.

children.text: Arbitrageurs: Closing the Gaps

markDefs.definition: A participant who simultaneously buys in one market and sells in another to lock in a price difference, taking little or no directional price risk.

children.text: An
arbitrageur

looks for the same commodity trading at inconsistent prices and buys the cheap one while selling the expensive one. If you know how equity arbitrage mutual funds work, this is the same idea applied to commodities.

The most common version is cash and carry. A futures price should roughly equal today's spot price plus the cost of holding the commodity until expiry, mainly the interest you give up on your money, plus storage and insurance.

body.caption: F is the fair futures price, S is the spot price, r is the annual interest rate and d is the number of days to expiry. You will study this cost of carry in Chapter 2.

children.text: Say spot gold is ₹1,00,000 per 10 grams, interest is 7% a year and expiry is 73 days away. Ignoring storage for simplicity, fair value is ₹1,00,000 × (1 + 0.07 × 73 ÷ 365) = ₹1,00,000 × 1.014 = ₹1,01,400. If the futures trade at ₹1,02,000, they are ₹600 too expensive. An arbitrageur buys physical gold at ₹1,00,000, sells futures at ₹1,02,000 and delivers the gold at expiry, earning ₹2,000 against a ₹1,400 funding cost.

body.title: The arbitrage profit
body.prompt: Using the example above, the arbitrageur earns ₹600 per 10 grams before transaction costs. How much is that for 1 kg of gold, in rupees?
body.explanation: 1 kg is 100 times 10 grams, so ₹600 × 100 = ₹60,000 before costs. In practice, GST on physical gold, brokerage, transaction charges and vaulting costs eat much of this, which is why such gaps are usually captured by bullion dealers and institutions with the lowest costs.

body.text: Arbitrageurs rarely make headlines, but they do something vital. By buying what is cheap and selling what is expensive, they push the two prices back together. This is a big reason MCX gold prices stay closely linked to international gold prices converted into rupees.

children.text: Who Is Actually Trading on MCX?
SEBI requires commodity exchanges to publish open interest data by participant category, so you can see who holds positions in each commodity.

body.caption: Participant categories in Indian commodity derivatives data

cells: Individual farmers and farmer producer organisations
Jewellers, processors, stockists, traders, importers and exporters
Brokers and firms trading their own money
Mutual funds, portfolio managers and similar institutions
Eligible foreign entities permitted by SEBI

body.label: A sobering number from SEBI
body.value: 93% of individual equity F&O traders lost money
body.context: SEBI's September 2024 study covered equity derivatives from FY22 to FY24, not commodities, but the lesson carries over: in leveraged derivatives, before costs one side's gain is the other side's loss, and after costs, most individual speculators end up on the losing side.

body.text: When you trade futures as a speculator, the person on the other side may be a hedger who is happy to lose on futures, or a professional with better data, faster execution and lower costs. Futures are a zero-sum game before costs and a negative-sum game after them. Your edge has to be real, not hopeful.

body.title: Name the participant
body.question: A cotton spinning mill in Coimbatore has signed a contract to deliver yarn at a fixed price in four months and buys cotton futures to protect itself. What kind of participant is it?
options: A speculator, because it is betting cotton will rise
A hedger taking a long hedge
A hedger taking a short hedge
body.explanation: The mill will need to buy cotton later and has already fixed its selling price, so a rise in cotton would hurt it. Buying futures offsets that risk, which is a long hedge. It is not speculating, because the futures position offsets an exposure it already has.

body.title: The hedger's goal
body.textWithBlank: A hedger uses futures not to make extra profit but to make the outcome ___.
body.explanation: Hedging trades away the chance of a windfall in exchange for removing the risk of a big loss. The measure of a good hedge is predictability, not futures profit.

body.title: Did Kantibhai make a mistake?
body.scenario: Kantibhai sold NCDEX jeera futures covering his 100 quintals at ₹24,000 per quintal. An unseasonal rain spell damaged the crop in Rajasthan and Gujarat, and jeera rose to ₹30,000 by the time he sold. His neighbour, who did not hedge, boasts that he made ₹6,00,000 more than Kantibhai on the same quantity. Kantibhai's son says hedging was a foolish waste.
body.prompt: Was the hedge a mistake? Explain what actually happened and how Kantibhai should think about it.
body.modelAnswer:
What happened: his physical stock gained (₹30,000 minus ₹24,000) × 100 = ₹6,00,000, and his short futures lost the same ₹6,00,000. He effectively sold at ₹24,000, the price he locked in. The neighbour gained ₹6,00,000 more because he stayed exposed to price risk.

Was it a mistake? No. The hedge did exactly its job: it fixed his selling price. The neighbour was not smarter, he was speculating with his stock. If prices had fallen to ₹18,000 instead, the neighbour would have lost ₹6,00,000 while Kantibhai would still have got ₹24,000.

How to think about it: judge a hedge by whether it protected the business against an outcome it could not afford, not by comparing it with hindsight. A better question for next season is how much of his stock to hedge, since hedging 50% or 70% keeps some upside while still protecting against a crash.

cards.definition: Uses futures to offset price risk from an existing physical business exposure.
Buying futures to protect against a price rise in a commodity you will need to buy.
Selling futures to protect against a price fall in a commodity you own or will produce.
Takes futures positions with no physical exposure, purely to profit from price moves.
Buys in one market and sells in another at the same time to lock in a price gap.
The difference between the local spot price and the futures price.
Buying the physical commodity and selling futures when futures are priced above spot plus carrying costs.
How easily you can trade without moving the price, supplied largely by speculators.

points: Hedgers use futures to remove price risk they already face: a long hedge protects a future buyer, a short hedge protects a holder or producer.
A good hedge makes outcomes predictable. Futures losses offset by physical gains are not a mistake.
Basis risk means real-world hedges are close, but never perfect.
Speculators take on the risk hedgers shed and supply the liquidity that makes markets work.
Arbitrageurs lock in price gaps, such as futures priced above spot plus carrying costs, and keep markets linked.
Futures are zero-sum before costs. Most retail traders are speculators, often facing better-informed and lower-cost participants.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment advice. All prices used are illustrative. Commodity derivatives are leveraged and can cause losses larger than your initial margin. Consult a SEBI-registered investment adviser before trading.
